title: Surrey mom killed by police was 'doing everything refugees are asked to do'
article: Warning: This story discusses intimate partner violence that may be triggering for some readers.

Vanessa Rentería Valencia was set to start English classes at a local non-profit this week - just days after the 37-year-old Surrey woman was shot dead by the police in her home in the early hours of Sept. 19.

The Pacific Immigrant Resources Society (PIRS) stated in a post on its website that Rentería Valencia had been attending the society's outreach programs. An Afro-Colombian newcomer to Canada, she was scheduled to start English classes this week. PIRS said she was "eager to integrate and advance her future."

"Those who worked with her remember a kind-hearted woman, devoted to her child, with clear dreams of moving forward. She actively sought community support to help her settle in her new home," the post read.

PIRS is one of numerous advocacy groups and community organizations that have spoken up since Renteria Valencia's death, which happened after Surrey RCMP received a call about a "disturbance" at a home in Cloverdale at about 4:40 a.m. last Thursday (Sept. 19).

Police say a woman had barricaded herself in a room with a toddler and was allegedly holding a weapon near the child. Less than an hour later, at about 5:30 a.m., an officer shot Renteria Valencia, who died at the scene. The Independent Investigations Office (IIO) - the independent civilian oversight agency that investigates all officer-related incidents that result in serious harm or death - is now investigating.

At a news conference at Surrey Libraries City Centre branch this Thursday (Sept. 26), several groups and organizations gathered to expose how the system failed Rentería Valencia on multiple fronts before that fatal confrontation.

Brian Seremba from BC Community Alliance - an organization dedicated to addressing the structural inequities caused by racism, particularly anti-Black racism - said the group is calling for a complete and transparent review "of the practices that led" to Rentería Valencia's death to prevent this from ever happening again.

"Vanessa was a daughter, a friend, an integral part of our fabric that binds us all. Her life was cut short and we demand justice and transparency throughout the entire investigation," Seremba said. "Police are more than equipped to deal with different types of crisis, and to see a member of our community that was shot and killed in front of her baby is devastating and tragic, and this calls for the community to cast a public outcry for the harms that have been caused to our community today."

Rentería Valencia came to Canada in 2022 and was "doing everything that a refugee is asked to do," Rosa Elena Arteaga, with Battered Women's Support Services, said. She volunteered, was learning English, and was a loving mother.
"She went to a shelter when she felt unsafe at home. She did everything that we asked women to do when they are not safe at home, we tell them to leave," Arteaga said.

Advocates said that Renteria Valencia had, for at least two months, been staying in a temporary shelter but had left the shelter in late August and returned to the home where she lived with her husband and brother-in-law.

It is believed that the week she died, she went to a friend and told them she wanted to leave her home as she did not feel safe. Renteria Valencia went back to her home on Sept. 18 to retrieve some belongings, and when she did not return to her friend's home, the friend called the police to check on her, Arteaga said.

The Surrey Now-Leader contacted the Surrey RCMP and IIO to confirm whether police had visited Renteria Valencia's residence in Cloverdale the day before she died. Both the RCMP and the IIO have refused further comment since the matter is now under investigation.

"We want to know the truth, but we are so tired to witness that women are criminalized and punished because of their gender, because of their ethnicity, because of being poor, because they don't speak English."
Renteria Valencia spoke Spanish, and advocates are asking whether the RCMP had an interpreter onsite or if the commands were given in Spanish.

Vanessa's father, in an interview with Colombian news media outlet Noticias al Instante Buenaventura, said, "in this moment, we are destroyed." He wants Colombian authorities to investigate the case because Canadian authorities aren't providing clear information. He said his daughter was a "noble and calm girl; she was not a girl of the street, she was a home girl, had been in Canada two years and her child is Canadian."

Sandra Renteria, Vanessa's sister, penned a letter to the Colombian government and the Colombian Consulate in Vancouver for assistance in obtaining a visa for family members to travel to Canada and in repatriating Renteria's body back to Colombia. The family is also calling for an "impartial and fair investigation" into her death.
If you or someone you know needs help with an abusive home situation, resources are available:
SURREY WOMEN'S CENTRE
Surrey Women's Centre is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week to support women and girls facing gender-based violence and to help care for women and children escaping violence.
BATTERED WOMEN'S SUPPORT SERVICES
BWSS offers support and assistance for those in crisis, including community resources and referrals to transition houses, lawyers and medical services.
